summary: Defines a set of SNMP managed objects for monitoring and configuring traffic engineering in MPLS networks, such as the tunnels operators set up to steer traffic along chosen paths. It lets standard network management tools read and manage this state in a uniform way.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a control panel with labeled dials for a network's special reserved roads. This document says what the dials are called, so any manager's tools can read them.

subtitle: The SNMP objects that let operators create, inspect and monitor MPLS traffic engineering tunnels in a uniform way.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering tunnels are explicitly routed paths set up across a network, and every vendor could expose their configuration and state differently.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3812 defines the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB, a set of SNMP tables for tunnels, their resources, requested, actual and computed hops, performance counters and CR-LDP resources, plus four notifications and a mapping of tunnels onto the interfaces table.
tldr.outcome: Management tools can configure and monitor MPLS TE tunnels the same way across devices, used together with the companion LSR MIB in RFC 3813. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3812 is a Proposed Standard from June 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read with RFC 3813.

sections.title: What the MPLS TE MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3812 defines managed objects for modelling traffic engineering (TE) in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) networks, as described in RFC 3031. It is meant to be used together with its companion, the MPLS Label Switching Router MIB in RFC 3813. The module is written in SMIv2 and accessed through SNMP.

In this document an explicitly routed LSP is called an MPLS tunnel. At an ingress or egress router it consists of in-segments and/or out-segments, and at an intermediate router one or more in-segments are joined to out-segments by a cross-connect. Those segment and cross-connect objects live in RFC 3813, not here.

The objects support the signalling described in RFC 3209 (RSVP-TE) and RFC 3212 (CR-LDP), and the tables support both manually configured and signalled tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel here is a road the network manager picked on purpose instead of letting traffic wander. This document is the list of settings and gauges for those roads.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The module is designed around a short list of requirements and constraints:

  • It configures point-to-point unidirectional tunnels.
  • Tunnels need not be interfaces, but a tunnel can be configured as one.
  • Tunnels can be set up by an MPLS signalling protocol, with parameters given at the head end of the LSP and the end-to-end LSP established by signalling. Manually configured tunnels are also supported, where an administrator provisions the label associations at each hop through the LSR MIB.
  • Both persistent and non-persistent tunnels are supported.

Only point-to-point tunnels are supported in the tunnel table, although multipoint-to-point and point-to-multipoint connections can be handled by a router acting as a cross-connect. Each tunnel can have one out-segment originating at a router and/or one in-segment terminating there.
sections.plainLanguage: The roads in this model go one way from one place to another. They can be built by hand or set up by routers talking to each other, and they can last or be temporary.

sections.title: The Tunnel Tables
sections.content:
The module is organised into tables that cross-reference one another:

  • mplsTunnelTable creates, reconfigures and removes tunnels between a router and a remote endpoint. It does not define the in and out segments; it refers to them through a cross-connect index.
  • mplsTunnelResourceTable describes the resources a tunnel needs. Several tunnels may share one entry, and tunnels that do not share resources must point to separate entries.
  • mplsTunnelHopTable holds the requested strict or loose hops, which several tunnels may share. The scalar mplsTunnelMaxHops gives the maximum number of hops per tunnel on the device.
  • mplsTunnelARHopTable reports the actual hops traversed, as reported by signalling after setup. It is optional, since not every signalling protocol supports it.
  • mplsTunnelCHopTable lists the hops computed by a constraint-based routing algorithm. It is also optional.
  • mplsTunnelPerfTable augments the tunnel table with performance counters.
  • mplsTunnelCRLDPResTable is a sparse extension of the resource table for tunnels signalled with CR-LDP, and may be supported only by implementations that support that protocol.

A tunnel entry records fields such as its ingress and egress router IDs, name, description, signalling protocol (none, rsvp, crldp or other), setup and holding priorities (each 0 to 7), and a role of head, transit, tail or headTail. Scalars report how many tunnels are configured and how many are active, and which TE distribution protocols the router uses (other, ospf or isis).
sections.plainLanguage: Think of several spreadsheets that point at each other. One lists the roads, one lists how much room each road needs, and others list the towns each road passes through, the towns it really passed through, and how much traffic it carried.

sections.title: Setting Up a Tunnel and Using RowPointer
sections.content:
Section 9 of the RFC walks through creating a best effort, loosely routed, unidirectional tunnel that spans two hops, with all objects created on the head-end router. The example fills in a resource entry, two hop entries (using the example addresses 192.168.100.1 and 192.168.101.1) and finally the tunnel entry, each created with a row status of createAndGo(4). Further instances of the active or signalled tunnel keep the same mplsTunnelIndex but have an mplsTunnelInstance greater than 0.

Two tunnel fields, mplsTunnelXCPointer and mplsTunnelResourcePointer, are of type RowPointer. They MUST point to the first instance of the first accessible column of the target row, so a manager can find the matching entry in the LSR MIB (the cross-connect, which is the LSP for the tunnel) or in a traffic parameter table such as the resource table. A value of zeroDotZero means no LSP, or no QoS resource, is associated with that tunnel instance.

The module can also send four notifications: mplsTunnelUp, mplsTunnelDown, mplsTunnelRerouted and mplsTunnelReoptimized. The up and down traps are sent only when mplsTunnelNotificationEnable is true (default false). mplsTunnelNotificationMaxRate caps notifications per second, and 0 means no throttling.
sections.plainLanguage: To build a road you first fill in a form for how much room it needs, then a list of towns, then the road itself. Each form has a pointer to the others so the manager can find them again.

sections.title: Interfaces and Counter Sizes
sections.content:
A tunnel can be a logical interface in the Interfaces Group of RFC 2863 (see RFC 2863). The interface stack puts an MPLS tunnel interface (ifType 150, mplsTunnel) above an MPLS interface (ifType 166, mpls), which sits above an underlying layer such as ATM, Frame Relay or Ethernet. The RFC lists how each ifTable object is read for a tunnel. ifName is the tunnel's name and ifConnectorPresent is false. ifPhysAddress is unused, ifOperStatus is down(2) when the tunnel is down, and ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable defaults to disabled.

The performance table offers 64-bit counters for fast links, and repeats the rule from RFC 2863. At 20,000,000 bits per second or less, 32-bit byte and packet counters MUST be supported. Above that and below 650,000,000 bits per second, 32-bit packet counters and 64-bit octet counters MUST be supported. At 650,000,000 bits per second or faster, 64-bit packet and octet counters MUST be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel can be treated like any other network connection on a router's list, so the same old tools can count its traffic. Fast roads need bigger counters so the numbers do not run out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that anything configurable can be misconfigured, with potentially disastrous results. The read-write and read-create objects are sensitive: the tunnel, hop, resource and CR-LDP resource tables together provision tunnels, so unauthorised access could disrupt traffic, especially once a tunnel is established. SNMPv3 VACM and USM MUST be used with any v3 agent that implements this MIB.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. The tunnel, hop, resource, performance and CR-LDP tables together reveal the MPLS TE topology and its performance, so an administrator who does not want that exposed should treat them as sensitive.

SNMP before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, even on a secure network. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever can change these settings can close or redirect the special roads, so only trusted people should hold the keys, and the map of the roads should not be public either.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
MPLS standards-track MIB modules are rooted under the mplsStdMIB subtree, and new assignments there can only be made through a Standards Action. The IANA assigned { mplsStdMIB 3 } to the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB module defined in this document.

The RFC notes that it contains four MPLS MIB modules in total, each with its own IANA subsection requesting an assignment, and this explainer covers the TE one.
sections.plainLanguage: The module was given its own official number in the big address book of network settings, so nobody else uses the same one.
